items.stem: What is the original source of energy for almost all ecosystems?
items.answer: The Sun
items.markingKey: The Sun. Producers capture solar energy.

items.stem: Distinguish between biotic factors and abiotic factors.
items.answer: Biotic factors are living parts of an ecosystem (plants, animals, microbes); abiotic factors are non-living (climate, soil, water, light).
items.markingKey: Biotic factors are living parts of an ecosystem (plants, animals, microbes); abiotic factors are non-living (climate, soil, water, light). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why decomposers are essential to ecosystems.
items.answer: They break down dead organisms and waste, releasing nutrients back into the soil so producers can use them; without them nutrients would be locked in dead matter.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They break down dead organisms and waste, releasing nutrients back into the soil so producers can use them; without them nutrients would be locked in dead matter. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A – National park report (paraphrased): Summary of US National Park Service information and research on wolves in Yellowstone, 2010s–2020s

After wolves were reintroduced in 1995, the park's elk population declined and elk spent less time grazing along streams. Researchers recorded recovery of willow and aspen in some areas, though scientists still debate how much of this was caused by wolves and how much by drought, bears and human hunting.

What is the message of Source A about ecosystems: food chains, nutrient cycles and biotic and abiotic factors? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: Wolves changed elk behaviour and helped some vegetation recover, though other factors also mattered.
items.markingKey: Wolves changed elk behaviour and helped some vegetation recover, though other factors also mattered. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How do abiotic factors (light, soil moisture and temperature) differ between the woodland edge and centre in our local park?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Use a transect from edge to centre; measure light, soil moisture and temperature every 5 m on three days; record; graph; relate to plant cover; evaluate equipment accuracy.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use a transect from edge to centre; measure light, soil moisture and temperature every 5 m on three days; record; graph; relate to plant cover; evaluate equipment accuracy. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What is an ecosystem?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into ecosystems: food chains, nutrient cycles and biotic and abiotic factors. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question Improved: "How do abiotic factors (light, soil moisture and temperature) differ between the woodland edge and centre in our local park?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How do abiotic factors (light, soil moisture and temperature) differ between the woodland edge and centre in our local park?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: In a tropical rainforest, where are most nutrients stored?
items.answer: In the biomass (living plants)
items.markingKey: C. Soils are poor because nutrients are recycled quickly.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Rainforests have very fertile soil." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most rainforest soils are poor; nutrients are mainly held in the vegetation.
items.markingKey: Most rainforest soils are poor; nutrients are mainly held in the vegetation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A rainforest food chain is: fig trees → fruit bats → snakes → harpy eagles. The fig trees store 50,000 kJ of energy per m² per year and 10% is transferred at each step. Calculate the energy at each trophic level and explain why there are few top predators.
items.answer: fig trees: 5e+04 kJ; fruit bats: 5,000 kJ; snakes: 500 kJ; harpy eagles: 50 kJ
items.markingKey: Multiply by 0.1 at each step (M1): fig trees: 5e+04 kJ; fruit bats: 5,000 kJ; snakes: 500 kJ; harpy eagles: 50 kJ (A2). Explanation (R1): energy is lost at each level, so only small populations of top consumers can be supported.

items.stem:
Source A – National park report (paraphrased): Summary of US National Park Service information and research on wolves in Yellowstone, 2010s–2020s

After wolves were reintroduced in 1995, the park's elk population declined and elk spent less time grazing along streams. Researchers recorded recovery of willow and aspen in some areas, though scientists still debate how much of this was caused by wolves and how much by drought, bears and human hunting.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching ecosystems: food chains, nutrient cycles and biotic and abiotic factors? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of US National Park Service information and research on wolves in Yellowstone, 2010s–2020s. Purpose: to inform the public about wolf restoration and its ecological effects. Value: It is based on long-term monitoring by park scientists. Limitation: It acknowledges scientific debate, so the size of the wolf effect is uncertain.
items.markingKey: Origin: Summary of US National Park Service information and research on wolves in Yellowstone, 2010s–2020s. Purpose: to inform the public about wolf restoration and its ecological effects. Value: It is based on long-term monitoring by park scientists. Limitation: It acknowledges scientific debate, so the size of the wolf effect is uncertain. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A biome receiving less than about 250 mm of rain a year, with high daytime temperatures and sparse vegetation"?
items.answer: hot desert
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of hot desert.

items.stem: "The rainforest is the "lungs of the Earth" and produces most of our oxygen." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rainforests use much of the oxygen they produce; most atmospheric oxygen comes from ocean phytoplankton. Rainforests matter greatly for carbon storage and rainfall.
items.markingKey: Rainforests use much of the oxygen they produce; most atmospheric oxygen comes from ocean phytoplankton. Rainforests matter greatly for carbon storage and rainfall. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why tundra plants are small and grow close to the ground.
items.answer: Low growth avoids strong, cold winds, keeps plants under insulating snow in winter and close to the warmer ground surface; permafrost also stops deep roots. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Low growth avoids strong, cold winds, keeps plants under insulating snow in winter and close to the warmer ground surface; permafrost also stops deep roots. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What are biomes?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into global biomes: tropical rainforests, hot deserts and tundra. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question Improved: "How have the Inuit of Nunavut adapted their way of life to the tundra, and how is climate change affecting this?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How have the Inuit of Nunavut adapted their way of life to the tundra, and how is climate change affecting this?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why hot deserts have a large daily temperature range.
items.answer: Clear skies and dry air let the Sun heat the ground strongly by day and let heat escape quickly at night, so days are very hot and nights can be cold.
items.markingKey: Content: Clear skies and dry air let the Sun heat the ground strongly by day and let heat escape quickly at night, so days are very hot and nights can be cold. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Justify the relevance of the research question "How have the Inuit of Nunavut adapted their way of life to the tundra, and how is climate change affecting this?"
items.answer: It links biome characteristics with human adaptation and change, using Indigenous perspectives.
items.markingKey: It links biome characteristics with human adaptation and change, using Indigenous perspectives. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Scientific assessment (paraphrased): Summary of findings in the IPCC "Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate", 2019

Permafrost soils in the Northern Hemisphere contain about 1 500 billion tonnes of carbon, roughly twice as much as is currently in the atmosphere. As the Arctic warms, thawing permafrost could release carbon dioxide and methane, adding to global warming.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about global biomes: tropical rainforests, hot deserts and tundra. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of findings in the IPCC "Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate", 2019. Purpose: to inform governments of the scientific evidence on climate change in cold regions. Value: It summarises peer-reviewed research agreed by scientists and governments. Limitation: Estimates of carbon stored and future release have wide uncertainty ranges.
items.markingKey: Origin: Summary of findings in the IPCC "Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate", 2019. Purpose: to inform governments of the scientific evidence on climate change in cold regions. Value: It summarises peer-reviewed research agreed by scientists and governments. Limitation: Estimates of carbon stored and future release have wide uncertainty ranges. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 4), scaled to the marks: 7-8 discusses concepts, issues and theories in detail, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses and evaluates a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and interprets different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Tropical rainforests are the most important biome to protect." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Rainforests have a strong claim because of biodiversity and carbon, but all biomes provide vital services; tundra protection is equally urgent for climate.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they hold the most land biodiversity and store huge amounts of carbon; they influence regional and global rainfall. Counter-arguments: tundra permafrost stores even more carbon, which may be released as it thaws; deserts and grasslands support unique species and millions of people. Thesis/conclusion: Rainforests have a strong claim because of biodiversity and carbon, but all biomes provide vital services; tundra protection is equally urgent for climate. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Briefly explain why tropical rainforests have such high biodiversity.
items.answer: Constant warmth, high rainfall and sunlight allow plants to grow all year, the layered structure creates many niches, and the biome has been stable for millions of years.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Constant warmth, high rainfall and sunlight allow plants to grow all year, the layered structure creates many niches, and the biome has been stable for millions of years. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between Arctic tundra and Alpine tundra.
items.answer: Arctic tundra lies at high latitudes around the Arctic Ocean, with permafrost; Alpine tundra occurs above the tree line on high mountains at any latitude and often lacks permafrost.
items.markingKey: Arctic tundra lies at high latitudes around the Arctic Ocean, with permafrost; Alpine tundra occurs above the tree line on high mountains at any latitude and often lacks permafrost. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Using the climate figures for Mumbai (India) below, suggest which climate zone it belongs to and justify your answer with two pieces of evidence from the data.
Month: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec
Temp (°C): 24 25 27 28 30 29 28 27 28 28 27 25
Rain (mm): 1 1 0 1 11 537 830 500 326 62 15 6
items.answer: Range 6 °C, total rain 2,290 mm; zone justified from these figures (see key).
items.markingKey: Evidence must be quoted: mean 27.2 °C, range 6 °C, total 2,290 mm, wettest July. Expected zone: tropical monsoon (hot all year, very wet June–September, dry winter). 1 mark zone, up to 3 marks for data-based justification.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Tropical rainforests are the most important biome to protect."
items.answer: Rainforests have a strong claim because of biodiversity and carbon, but all biomes provide vital services; tundra protection is equally urgent for climate.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they hold the most land biodiversity and store huge amounts of carbon; they influence regional and global rainfall. Arguments against: tundra permafrost stores even more carbon, which may be released as it thaws; deserts and grasslands support unique species and millions of people. Supported judgement: Rainforests have a strong claim because of biodiversity and carbon, but all biomes provide vital services; tundra protection is equally urgent for climate. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 4), scaled to the marks: 7-8 discusses concepts, issues and theories in detail, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses and evaluates a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and interprets different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which activity is the largest single driver of deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon?
items.answer: Cattle ranching
items.markingKey: C. Pasture occupies most cleared land.

items.stem: Explain the difference between forest degradation and deforestation.
items.answer: Deforestation removes forest completely and converts land to another use; degradation reduces forest quality (by selective logging or fire) while it remains forest.
items.markingKey: Deforestation removes forest completely and converts land to another use; degradation reduces forest quality (by selective logging or fire) while it remains forest. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why deforestation can reduce rainfall in the Amazon.
items.answer: Trees return large amounts of water to the air through transpiration; when forest is cleared, less moisture is recycled, so rainfall downwind falls and dry seasons lengthen.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Trees return large amounts of water to the air through transpiration; when forest is cleared, less moisture is recycled, so rainfall downwind falls and dry seasons lengthen. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A – Space agency data (paraphrased): Summary of annual PRODES data from Brazil's National Institute for Space Research (INPE)

Brazil's PRODES satellite monitoring recorded about 27 800 km² of clearing in the Legal Amazon in 2004, falling to about 4 600 km² in 2012. Clearing then rose, reaching about 13 000 km² in 2021, before falling again to about 9 000 km² in 2023.

What is the message of Source A about threats to ecosystems: deforestation, desertification and biodiversity loss? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: Deforestation fell sharply after 2004, rose after 2012 and fell again recently.
items.markingKey: Deforestation fell sharply after 2004, rose after 2012 and fell again recently. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "Why did Amazon deforestation in Brazil fall between 2004 and 2012 and then rise again?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Download PRODES data; draw a line graph; research policies (PPCDAm, soy moratorium) and later changes; read two analyses; link causes to the trend; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Download PRODES data; draw a line graph; research policies (PPCDAm, soy moratorium) and later changes; read two analyses; link causes to the trend; evaluate sources; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Deforestation is the greatest threat to global biodiversity." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Land-use change, including deforestation, is currently the largest driver on land, but climate change may become the greatest threat overall, and the drivers interact.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: tropical forests hold most land species and are being cleared rapidly; land-use change is ranked the top driver by IPBES. Counter-arguments: climate change is a growing threat to all ecosystems, including oceans and coral reefs; over-exploitation, pollution and invasive species also cause major losses. Thesis/conclusion: Land-use change, including deforestation, is currently the largest driver on land, but climate change may become the greatest threat overall, and the drivers interact. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A species introduced to a new area where it spreads and harms native species"?
items.answer: invasive species
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of invasive species.

items.stem: The data show the area of the Aral Sea (approx., satellite and survey data): 1960: 68 thousand km²; 1980: 51 thousand km²; 1990: 36 thousand km²; 2000: 25 thousand km²; 2010: 14 thousand km². Calculate the average rate of change per year between 1960 and 2000, and per decade.
items.answer: -1.07 thousand km² per year (-10.8 per decade)

items.stem: A student chose the research question "Why did Amazon deforestation in Brazil fall between 2004 and 2012 and then rise again?" Explain two reasons why this question is relevant and worth investigating.
items.answer: It investigates change over time and the effect of policy, using INPE data and reports.
items.markingKey: It investigates change over time and the effect of policy, using INPE data and reports. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Define the term "rewilding".
items.answer: Restoring natural processes and species, such as predators, to an area and reducing human management
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: restoring natural processes and species, such as predators, to an area and reducing human management. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Planting trees anywhere always helps the environment." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Planting the wrong species, or trees on natural grasslands, can harm biodiversity and water supplies; restoring native ecosystems is better.
items.markingKey: Planting the wrong species, or trees on natural grasslands, can harm biodiversity and water supplies; restoring native ecosystems is better. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between conservation and preservation.
items.answer: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources while protecting them; preservation aims to keep areas untouched with minimal human use.
items.markingKey: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources while protecting them; preservation aims to keep areas untouched with minimal human use. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the Great Green Wall and explain what it reveals about large-scale restoration of degraded land.
items.answer: Launched by the African Union in 2007, it aims to restore 100 million hectares across the Sahel by 2030; progress has been uneven, with Ethiopia and Senegal among the most active. It shows both the ambition and the funding and coordination challenges of restoration.
items.markingKey: Context (Launched by the African Union in 2007, it aims to restore 100 million hectares across the Sahel by 2030; progress has been uneven, with Ethiopia and Senegal among the most active.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows both the ambition and the funding and coordination challenges of restoration. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to large-scale restoration of degraded land.

items.stem:
Source A – Nobel lecture (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2004

The speaker explained that the movement began by encouraging rural women in Kenya to plant trees to meet their needs for firewood, clean water and food. Over time, she said, they understood that environmental destruction was linked to poor governance and that protecting the environment also meant defending democracy and peace.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Tree planting by women met local needs and grew into a movement for democracy and peace.
items.markingKey: Tree planting by women met local needs and grew into a movement for democracy and peace. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "National parks are the most effective way to protect ecosystems." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Parks are important, but they work best when combined with community involvement and wider sustainable land use outside their borders.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: strict protection has saved species such as Kaziranga's rhinos; parks provide refuges and tourism income. Counter-arguments: parks can exclude local people and suffer from poor enforcement ("paper parks"); community conservancies, PES schemes and Indigenous land rights can be as or more effective. Thesis/conclusion: Parks are important, but they work best when combined with community involvement and wider sustainable land use outside their borders. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Explain why involving local communities improves conservation.
items.answer: Local people know the land, depend on its resources and can monitor it; if they benefit (jobs, income, rights), they support conservation rather than resisting or ignoring it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Local people know the land, depend on its resources and can monitor it; if they benefit (jobs, income, rights), they support conservation rather than resisting or ignoring it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

options: How effective has Costa Rica's payments for ecosystem services programme been in increasing forest cover since 1997?
items.answer: How effective has Costa Rica's payments for ecosystem services programme been in increasing forest cover since 1997?
items.markingKey: A. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.answer: Weakness: it is very broad and vague Improved: "How effective has Costa Rica's payments for ecosystem services programme been in increasing forest cover since 1997?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is very broad and vague); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How effective has Costa Rica's payments for ecosystem services programme been in increasing forest cover since 1997?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Tropical rainforests cover about 6% of the land surface. Roughly what share of land species do they contain?
items.answer: More than half
items.markingKey: A. They are the most biodiverse land biome.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "trophic level"?
options: The position an organism occupies in a food chain
A UN-backed framework that pays developing countries to reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation
A biome receiving less than about 250 mm of rain a year, with high daytime temperatures and sparse vegetation
A large-scale ecosystem, such as tropical rainforest or tundra, defined mainly by climate and vegetation
items.answer: The position an organism occupies in a food chain
items.markingKey: A. "trophic level" is the position an organism occupies in a food chain.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "habitat fragmentation".
items.answer: The breaking up of a continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the breaking up of a continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between conservation and preservation.
items.answer: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources while protecting them; preservation aims to keep areas untouched with minimal human use.
items.markingKey: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources while protecting them; preservation aims to keep areas untouched with minimal human use. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between Alpine tundra and Arctic tundra.
items.answer: Arctic tundra lies at high latitudes around the Arctic Ocean, with permafrost; Alpine tundra occurs above the tree line on high mountains at any latitude and often lacks permafrost.
items.markingKey: Arctic tundra lies at high latitudes around the Arctic Ocean, with permafrost; Alpine tundra occurs above the tree line on high mountains at any latitude and often lacks permafrost. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why tropical rainforest soils are infertile despite lush vegetation.
items.answer: Heavy rain leaches nutrients from the soil, and dead material decomposes and is reabsorbed by plants so quickly that most nutrients are held in the biomass, not the soil.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Heavy rain leaches nutrients from the soil, and dead material decomposes and is reabsorbed by plants so quickly that most nutrients are held in the biomass, not the soil. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Deforestation in the Amazon is mainly caused by poor farmers cutting trees for firewood." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most clearing in Brazil is for large-scale cattle pasture and soy, linked to global markets and land speculation.
items.markingKey: Most clearing in Brazil is for large-scale cattle pasture and soy, linked to global markets and land speculation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why protecting large connected areas is better than small isolated reserves.
items.answer: Large, linked areas support bigger populations, allow animals to migrate and adapt to climate change, and keep ecological processes working.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Large, linked areas support bigger populations, allow animals to migrate and adapt to climate change, and keep ecological processes working. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Deserts have no life." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Deserts support many adapted plants and animals – cacti, acacias, camels, fennec foxes – and people such as the Tuareg.
items.markingKey: Deserts support many adapted plants and animals – cacti, acacias, camels, fennec foxes – and people such as the Tuareg. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into ecosystems: food chains, nutrient cycles and biotic and abiotic factors?
options: How do abiotic factors (light, soil moisture and temperature) differ between the woodland edge and centre in our local park?
items.answer: How do abiotic factors (light, soil moisture and temperature) differ between the woodland edge and centre in our local park?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: Sana argues that "Deforestation is the greatest threat to global biodiversity." Isabel disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Land-use change, including deforestation, is currently the largest driver on land, but climate change may become the greatest threat overall, and the drivers interact.
items.markingKey: Sana: tropical forests hold most land species and are being cleared rapidly. Isabel: climate change is a growing threat to all ecosystems, including oceans and coral reefs. Judgement (1-2 marks): Land-use change, including deforestation, is currently the largest driver on land, but climate change may become the greatest threat overall, and the drivers interact.

items.stem:
Source A – Nobel lecture (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2004

The speaker explained that the movement began by encouraging rural women in Kenya to plant trees to meet their needs for firewood, clean water and food. Over time, she said, they understood that environmental destruction was linked to poor governance and that protecting the environment also meant defending democracy and peace.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching conservation and the sustainable management of ecosystems? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2004. Purpose: to explain the Green Belt Movement and link environment, democracy and peace to an international audience. Value: It is the founder's own account of the movement's aims and growth. Limitation: As a Nobel lecture it presents the movement positively and gives little detail on measured outcomes.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2004. Purpose: to explain the Green Belt Movement and link environment, democracy and peace to an international audience. Value: It is the founder's own account of the movement's aims and growth. Limitation: As a Nobel lecture it presents the movement positively and gives little detail on measured outcomes. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 4), scaled to the marks: 7-8 discusses concepts, issues and theories in detail, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses and evaluates a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and interprets different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How have the Inuit of Nunavut adapted their way of life to the tundra, and how is climate change affecting this?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Read Inuit organisation reports and two secondary sources; watch an Inuit-produced documentary; record evidence in a table (traditional vs current); evaluate perspectives; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Read Inuit organisation reports and two secondary sources; watch an Inuit-produced documentary; record evidence in a table (traditional vs current); evaluate perspectives; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Felix argues that "Abiotic factors are more important than biotic factors in shaping ecosystems." Freya disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Abiotic factors set the broad limits, but biotic interactions – including human activity – strongly shape how ecosystems work within those limits.
items.markingKey: Felix: climate determines the global distribution of biomes. Freya: keystone species such as wolves and beavers reshape habitats. Judgement (1-2 marks): Abiotic factors set the broad limits, but biotic interactions – including human activity – strongly shape how ecosystems work within those limits.

items.stem:
Source A – Space agency data (paraphrased): Summary of annual PRODES data from Brazil's National Institute for Space Research (INPE)

Brazil's PRODES satellite monitoring recorded about 27 800 km² of clearing in the Legal Amazon in 2004, falling to about 4 600 km² in 2012. Clearing then rose, reaching about 13 000 km² in 2021, before falling again to about 9 000 km² in 2023.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching threats to ecosystems: deforestation, desertification and biodiversity loss? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of annual PRODES data from Brazil's National Institute for Space Research (INPE). Purpose: to provide official annual measurements of Amazon deforestation. Value: It is consistent, long-term satellite data used by scientists and governments. Limitation: It measures clear-cutting only, not degradation by fire or selective logging; political pressure on INPE has been reported.

items.stem: Data from approx., Costa Rican government: Costa Rica's forest cover – 1987: 21 per cent of land area; 2021: 57 per cent of land area. By what percentage did it change over the period? Show your working.
items.markingKey: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 (M1) = (57 − 21) ÷ 21 × 100 = +171.4% (A1). Dividing by the new value is a common error.

items.stem:
Source A – Scientific assessment (paraphrased): Summary of findings in the IPCC "Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate", 2019

Permafrost soils in the Northern Hemisphere contain about 1 500 billion tonnes of carbon, roughly twice as much as is currently in the atmosphere. As the Arctic warms, thawing permafrost could release carbon dioxide and methane, adding to global warming.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Tropical rainforests are the most important biome to protect."
items.answer: Rainforests have a strong claim because of biodiversity and carbon, but all biomes provide vital services; tundra protection is equally urgent for climate.
items.markingKey: From the source: Thawing tundra permafrost could release huge amounts of greenhouse gases. Own knowledge for: they hold the most land biodiversity and store huge amounts of carbon; they influence regional and global rainfall. Own knowledge against: tundra permafrost stores even more carbon, which may be released as it thaws; deserts and grasslands support unique species and millions of people. Judgement: Rainforests have a strong claim because of biodiversity and carbon, but all biomes provide vital services; tundra protection is equally urgent for climate. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem:
Source A – National park report (paraphrased): Summary of US National Park Service information and research on wolves in Yellowstone, 2010s–2020s

After wolves were reintroduced in 1995, the park's elk population declined and elk spent less time grazing along streams. Researchers recorded recovery of willow and aspen in some areas, though scientists still debate how much of this was caused by wolves and how much by drought, bears and human hunting.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Abiotic factors are more important than biotic factors in shaping ecosystems."
items.answer: Abiotic factors set the broad limits, but biotic interactions – including human activity – strongly shape how ecosystems work within those limits.
items.markingKey: From the source: Wolves changed elk behaviour and helped some vegetation recover, though other factors also mattered. Own knowledge for: climate determines the global distribution of biomes; soil, water and sunlight limit what can live in a place. Own knowledge against: keystone species such as wolves and beavers reshape habitats; humans, a biotic factor, now transform ecosystems everywhere. Judgement: Abiotic factors set the broad limits, but biotic interactions – including human activity – strongly shape how ecosystems work within those limits. items.stem:
Source A – Nobel lecture (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2004

The speaker explained that the movement began by encouraging rural women in Kenya to plant trees to meet their needs for firewood, clean water and food. Over time, she said, they understood that environmental destruction was linked to poor governance and that protecting the environment also meant defending democracy and peace.

"National parks are the most effective way to protect ecosystems." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Parks are important, but they work best when combined with community involvement and wider sustainable land use outside their borders.
items.markingKey: From the source: Tree planting by women met local needs and grew into a movement for democracy and peace. Own knowledge for: strict protection has saved species such as Kaziranga's rhinos; parks provide refuges and tourism income. Own knowledge against: parks can exclude local people and suffer from poor enforcement ("paper parks"); community conservancies, PES schemes and Indigenous land rights can be as or more effective. Judgement: Parks are important, but they work best when combined with community involvement and wider sustainable land use outside their borders. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "biodiversity"?
options: An organism, such as a fungus or bacterium, that breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the soil
The variety of life in an area – species, genes and ecosystems
Growing trees together with crops or livestock on the same land
A biome near the equator with high temperatures (about 27 °C) and rainfall above 2 000 mm all year, with layered, very diverse forest
items.answer: The variety of life in an area – species, genes and ecosystems
items.markingKey: B. "biodiversity" is the variety of life in an area – species, genes and ecosystems.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "trophic level".
items.answer: The position an organism occupies in a food chain
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the position an organism occupies in a food chain. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "invasive species"?
options: The protection and careful management of ecosystems, species and natural resources
The decline in the variety of species, genes and ecosystems
An area, such as a national park, where human activity is managed to conserve nature
A species introduced to a new area where it spreads and harms native species
items.answer: A species introduced to a new area where it spreads and harms native species
items.markingKey: D. "invasive species" is a species introduced to a new area where it spreads and harms native species.

items.stem: "Once a species is protected by law, it is safe." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Laws must be enforced and habitats protected; poaching, habitat loss and climate change continue to threaten protected species.
items.markingKey: Laws must be enforced and habitats protected; poaching, habitat loss and climate change continue to threaten protected species. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between Alpine tundra and Arctic tundra.
items.answer: Arctic tundra lies at high latitudes around the Arctic Ocean, with permafrost; Alpine tundra occurs above the tree line on high mountains at any latitude and often lacks permafrost.
items.markingKey: Arctic tundra lies at high latitudes around the Arctic Ocean, with permafrost; Alpine tundra occurs above the tree line on high mountains at any latitude and often lacks permafrost. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Leila writes: "Removing one species makes little difference to an ecosystem." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Species are interconnected; losing a keystone species can cause large changes (trophic cascades).
items.markingKey: Species are interconnected; losing a keystone species can cause large changes (trophic cascades). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Maya writes: "Deforestation in the Amazon is mainly caused by poor farmers cutting trees for firewood." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most clearing in Brazil is for large-scale cattle pasture and soy, linked to global markets and land speculation.
items.markingKey: Most clearing in Brazil is for large-scale cattle pasture and soy, linked to global markets and land speculation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between in-situ conservation and ex-situ conservation.
items.answer: In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat (national parks); ex-situ protects them outside it (zoos, seed banks such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault).
items.markingKey: In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat (national parks); ex-situ protects them outside it (zoos, seed banks such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Sana writes: "The rainforest is the "lungs of the Earth" and produces most of our oxygen." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rainforests use much of the oxygen they produce; most atmospheric oxygen comes from ocean phytoplankton. Rainforests matter greatly for carbon storage and rainfall.
items.markingKey: Rainforests use much of the oxygen they produce; most atmospheric oxygen comes from ocean phytoplankton. Rainforests matter greatly for carbon storage and rainfall. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.
items.answer: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level; the rest is lost as heat, movement and waste, so after a few levels there is too little energy to support another population.
items.markingKey: Content: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level; the rest is lost as heat, movement and waste, so after a few levels there is too little energy to support another population. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Using the Aral Sea as an example, explain human-caused ecosystem destruction.
items.answer: From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to irrigate cotton; the sea shrank by about 90%, its fishing industry collapsed and salty dust storms harmed health. Water use for one economic goal destroyed an entire aquatic ecosystem and livelihoods.
items.markingKey: Context (From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to irrigate cotton; the sea shrank by about 90%, its fishing industry collapsed and salty dust storms harmed health.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: water use for one economic goal destroyed an entire aquatic ecosystem and livelihoods. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to human-caused ecosystem destruction.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why "fortress conservation" has been criticised.
items.answer: Creating parks by removing Indigenous and local people from their land caused injustice and conflict, and ignored their role in caring for ecosystems.
items.markingKey: Content: Creating parks by removing Indigenous and local people from their land caused injustice and conflict, and ignored their role in caring for ecosystems. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. What is the message of Source A about global biomes: tropical rainforests, hot deserts and tundra? Refer to details in the source.

items.stem: A student chose the research question "How do abiotic factors (light, soil moisture and temperature) differ between the woodland edge and centre in our local park?" Explain two reasons why this question is relevant and worth investigating.
items.answer: It investigates abiotic variation with simple field measurements linked to ecosystem processes.
items.markingKey: It investigates abiotic variation with simple field measurements linked to ecosystem processes. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into threats to ecosystems: deforestation, desertification and biodiversity loss?
options: Why did Amazon deforestation in Brazil fall between 2004 and 2012 and then rise again?
items.answer: Why did Amazon deforestation in Brazil fall between 2004 and 2012 and then rise again?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How have the Inuit of Nunavut adapted their way of life to the tundra, and how is climate change affecting this?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Abiotic factors are more important than biotic factors in shaping ecosystems." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Abiotic factors set the broad limits, but biotic interactions – including human activity – strongly shape how ecosystems work within those limits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: climate determines the global distribution of biomes; soil, water and sunlight limit what can live in a place. Counter-arguments: keystone species such as wolves and beavers reshape habitats; humans, a biotic factor, now transform ecosystems everywhere. Thesis/conclusion: Abiotic factors set the broad limits, but biotic interactions – including human activity – strongly shape how ecosystems work within those limits. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Noah is investigating threats to ecosystems: deforestation, desertification and biodiversity loss and proposes the research question: "Is deforestation bad?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed question with an obvious answer Improved: "Why did Amazon deforestation in Brazil fall between 2004 and 2012 and then rise again?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed question with an obvious answer); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "Why did Amazon deforestation in Brazil fall between 2004 and 2012 and then rise again?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How effective has Costa Rica's payments for ecosystem services programme been in increasing forest cover since 1997?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Collect forest-cover data (FAO, national); read two studies on PES; consider other factors (cattle prices, tourism); graph change; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect forest-cover data (FAO, national); read two studies on PES; consider other factors (cattle prices, tourism); graph change; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
